description_full: LuxExperience B.V., through its subsidiary, operates digital platform for the luxury fashion in Germany, the United States, Europe, Middle East, Japan, mainland China, Hong Kong SAR, China, and internationally. The company offers womenswear, menswear, kidswear, fine jewelry, watches, fine jewelry and lifestyle products under the Mytheresa, NET-A-PORTER, MR PORTER, YOOX, and the OUTNET brand name. The company was formerly known as MYT Netherlands Parent B.V. and changed its name to LuxExperience B.V. in May 2025. LuxExperience B.V. was founded in 1987 and is based in Munich, Germany.

financial_summary: LuxExperience B.V. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $1.4B market cap on $1.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +21% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at -2% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 48%.
The company is burning through $37M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
Accruals are elevated at +25.4% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 79× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 87% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 5.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 46% operating margin runs 38pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 5.55x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 55% and a beta of 1.14, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.13 vs 5y 1.39), so read it loosely.
About $1.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 62% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 85%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of -2.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 49.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $11.05 on average, 8% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 2% falls short of the cost of capital of 10.4%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.84).
It runs a 48% gross margin and burns cash (FCF margin -3%).
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only -0.05x and high accruals (+25.4% of assets).
ROE of 40% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 38pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $471.9M.
Warning signs: a Beneish M-score that flags possible earnings manipulation, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 20.9% over 3 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 19%).
own: Insiders own 87.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 19%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (13 sales, net $4.9M sold).
The share count has grown 14.4% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
Short interest is elevated at 18.7% of the float, 9.9 days to cover.
people: With about 3,738 employees, each generates about $362K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 17.1% a year.
Free cash flow is negative, at -$10K per employee.
